title: Catégorie des types de mots [dont arbres plans] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page opens a section 'Arbres plans' (plane trees) inside a dossier on a 'category of types of words'. The previous page dealt with graphs carrying an involution on edges, defined recursively by contracting pairs of consecutive edges. Such involutive structures are close to chord diagrams, bracketings and Dyck-word combinatorics. Plane trees are presumably wanted as the combinatorial model for these word types.

(1) Combinatorial tree. A tree is a connected, simply connected ('1-connexe') combinatorial graph. Such a graph is automatically simple ('strict'): no loops and no multiple edges. So it can be encoded as a pair (S, A) with S a nonempty set of vertices and A a subset of P_2(S), the 2-element subsets of S. If A is empty then card S = 1 (the point tree).

(2) Plane tree, topologically. A plane tree is a tree together with a class of embeddings |Γ| -> X into a surface X. Two embeddings |Γ| -> X and |Γ| -> X' are identified if there are neighbourhoods U, U' of |Γ| and a homeomorphism U ≅ U' restricting to the identity on |Γ|. So the datum is the germ of the ambient surface along the tree, modulo homeomorphism rel the tree.

(3) Reduction to the disc. |Γ| is simply connected, so it has a simply connected open neighbourhood U ≅ R^2. Hence every such germ is a germ inside the plane, which justifies the word 'plan'.

(4) Combinatorial classification.
- For each vertex s, let A_s be the set of edges incident to s.
- circ(Γ) is the set of systems of cyclic orders on all the A_s. These are 'rotation systems'; the transcription's 'circonlocutions' is uncertain and may be 'circulations'.
- An embedding germ in an oriented surface corresponds to one element of circ(Γ).
- Without an orientation, a germ corresponds to a 'bi-' structure: a pair (E, c), with E a 2-element set (the two local orientations of the neighbourhood) and c: E -> circ(Γ) equivariant for the swap on E and global reversal of all cyclic orders.
- Equivalently, an unoriented plane tree is a rotation system up to global reversal, encoded as an E-torsor so as to keep track of automorphisms.

(5) Degenerate cases. The cyclic orders only carry information at vertices with card A_s ≥ 3. A cyclic order on a set with at most 2 elements is unique and equal to its reverse. So if all vertices have small degree, the plane structure exists and is unique; the text breaks off at 'il y en a ... et une seule'.

The page sets up the bridge between abstract trees, topological plane trees and rotation-system data. Presumably this is the groundwork for counting plane trees or relating them to word types. Plane trees are also the one-face dessins d'enfants (Shabat polynomials) that Grothendieck was studying in the same years.

Dating: the reverse of the next sheet is an IBM job log stamped 82139, i.e. 19 May 1982. The sheets were presumably used after that date, consistent with the archive's 'à partir de 1982'.
errors: Final sentence: the transcription reads 'sommets d'ordre ≤ 1'. The natural sharp statement is degree ≤ 2: all paths have a unique plane structure, since the cyclic order on ≤ 2 elements is unique and self-opposite. With ≤ 1 the statement is true but nearly vacuous (only the point and the segment). The handwriting may be '2'.

Minor gap: the existence of a simply connected neighbourhood homeomorphic to R^2 implicitly uses that X is a surface without boundary near |Γ|. It also uses the classification of simply connected open surfaces, or simply regular neighbourhoods; tameness is automatic in dimension 2 (Schoenflies). The claim is correct but stated tersely.
The 'compatible with the opposite' condition on c: E -> circ(Γ) should be read as equivariance for the swap on E and global reversal on circ(Γ). Otherwise the set of (E, c) would be too large.

ideas.what: Tree encoded as (S, A) with A ⊂ P_2(S); a simply connected graph is simple
Plane tree defined as a germ of embedding into a surface, modulo homeomorphisms of neighbourhoods fixing the tree
ideas.modern_name: ribbon (fat) graph structure / regular-neighbourhood germ of an embedded graph
ideas.usually_credited_to: Heffter (1891), Edmonds (1960); ribbon graphs in Penner, Kontsevich and others
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984) discusses cartes/dessins and plane trees, but not with this germ formalism as far as known

ideas.what: Embedding germs in oriented surfaces correspond bijectively to systems of cyclic orders on the edges at each vertex
ideas.modern_name: rotation systems (Heffter–Edmonds theorem, here in the simply connected case)

ideas.what: Unoriented plane structure as a pair (E, c), with E a 2-element orientation torsor and c an equivariant map to rotation systems
ideas.modern_name: rotation system up to global reversal, i.e. orientation double cover / Z/2-torsor formulation
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard in map theory (unoriented maps via flags, Tutte; Jones–Singerman)

ideas.what: Plane structure only matters at vertices of degree ≥ 3; paths have a unique plane structure

missed.claim: Dating evidence: the next sheet is computer paper with an IBM job log stamped 82139 (19 May 1982). This gives a terminus post quem for this batch of notes, placing Grothendieck's work on plane trees and word types after mid-May 1982. That is in the period leading to the Esquisse and the dessins d'enfants work.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Helps date Grothendieck's combinatorial work on plane trees relative to his dessins/Shabat-polynomial work and the Esquisse d'un programme (January 1984).

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a careful but standard setup: trees, plane trees as embedding germs, and their classification by rotation systems, with a torsor formulation of the unoriented case. All of this is classical map theory. The only modest points of interest are the torsor phrasing and the May 1982 dating clue from the paper.
transcription_corrections: 'bicirconlocutions' / 'circonlocutions' is uncertain in the image; it may be 'bicirculations' / 'circulations'. It denotes systems of cyclic orders (rotation systems) and is best treated as Grothendieck's ad hoc term.
'compatible avec "l'opposé"' likely reads 'compatible avec "passage à l'opposé"' (reversal of cyclic orders) or similar.
'ce n'est distinguant pas de l'autre feuille des Γ' is garbled. The sense is roughly that this structure (the choice between the two orientations) is only nontrivial at vertices with card A_s ≥ 3.
Final line: 'd'ordre ≤1' may be '≤ 2' (the mathematically natural bound); 'il y en a ... et une seule' should read 'il y en a une et une seule'.
'(classe isot. top.)' is the interlinear insertion after 'plongements'; the deleted words are 'dans une surface'.
